## Sources

In-house `zzcollab` framework at
`github.com/rgt47/zzcollab` (version 0.2.0 at the time
of writing).
Blog posts `14-penguins1zzcollab` and
`42-zzedcindependence`. This chapter describes
`zzcollab` as it exists at time of writing; check
the framework's `CHANGELOG.md` for current status.
:::

## Prerequisites

Answer the following questions to see if you can bypass
this chapter. You can find the answers at the end of the
chapter in @sec-quiz-answers-10.

1. What are the *Five Pillars* that `zzcollab`
   identifies as essential for a reproducible
   research compendium, and what does each pillar
   capture that the other four do not?
2. How does `zzcollab` relate to `rrtools`, `renv`,
   and Docker? Does it replace them, wrap them, or
   compose them?
3. What does a `zzcollab` profile determine, and when
   would you pick `publishing` over `tidyverse`?

## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- Scaffold a new research project with
  `zzc <profile>` in one command.
- Explain and audit the Five Pillars of a `zzcollab`
  compendium.
- Choose the appropriate profile (minimal,
  tidyverse, rstudio, publishing) for a given
  study.
- Use the project `Makefile` targets (`make r`,
  `make check-renv`, `make docker-render-qmd`) to
  interact with the container.
- Read how profiles are defined in
  `templates/bundles.yaml`, and judge where a
  research group's conventions belong.
- Recognize when `zzcollab` is overkill and when
  it is exactly the right level of infrastructure.

## Orientation

The three preceding chapters each solved one layer of the
reproducibility problem and each left the wiring to the reader.
A compendium does not come with a lockfile; a lockfile does not
come with a container; a container does not know where your
paper lives. Assembling the three by hand is about half an hour
of work per project. It is also exactly the kind of work that
gets done slightly differently every time, which defeats the
consistency it was supposed to produce.

`zzcollab` is an opinionated framework that does the assembly.
It packages the ideas of `rrtools`, `renv`, and Docker into a
single command-line workflow, trading flexibility for speed of
setup and for uniformity across a group's projects. The trade
is real in both directions and worth stating plainly. Every
project in the group looks the same, and a collaborator knows
where things live without asking. The price is rather less
control over the layout than bare `rrtools` would give you. A
reader who wants that control should use `rrtools` directly and
will lose nothing this book teaches.

The framework exists because the manual setup
(Dockerfile, renv, rrtools layout, Makefile
targets, check scripts) is roughly 30--60 minutes
of error-prone work per project. For a research
group that produces many projects, automating
that setup pays back quickly. For a one-off
analysis, plain `rrtools` (@sec-rrtools) suffices.

## The statistician's contribution {#sec-zzcollab-human}

The framework's whole purpose is to make the mechanical
parts disappear. What it cannot decide for you is
whether it should be used at all, and at what weight:

**Choose the right profile.** A manuscript that
must render to PDF needs LaTeX, which only the
`publishing` profile's base image has. A simple
descriptive analysis in the `publishing` profile
waits for a 4 GB image it does not need. The profile
is a substantive choice; defaulting to the heaviest
one wastes time, the lightest one wastes more time
when it fails to support what you need.

**Decide where conventions live.** A research group
has local conventions: a preferred database client, a
set of in-house packages, journal-specific Quarto
templates. Writing them down once, in a template
project or a shared lockfile, saves every downstream
project from re-enumerating them. The investment is
made once; the benefit compounds.

**Audit the Pillars.** `make check-renv` verifies
that the code, `DESCRIPTION`, and `renv.lock` agree
about packages; it does not check the Dockerfile,
`.Rprofile`, or data, so those need a manual look.
Skipping the audit before deposition or paper
submission is the kind of small omission that breaks
reproducibility years later.

**Recognize the limits.** `zzcollab` is not the
answer to every project. For interactive
exploration, RStudio alone is faster. For a
one-off script, scaffolding a compendium is
overhead. The skill is knowing which projects
warrant the framework.

These decisions are what distinguish using
`zzcollab` as a tool from using it as a ritual.

## The Five Pillars

`zzcollab` identifies five components as jointly
necessary for reproducibility. A compendium
missing any one is incomplete.

| Pillar           | Role                                           |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `Dockerfile`     | Operating system, system libraries, R build    |
| `renv.lock`      | Exact versions of every R package              |
| `.Rprofile`      | Project-local R configuration (activates renv) |
| Source code      | Analysis scripts and functions                 |
| Data             | Raw and processed data (or DOI pointers)       |

The pillars are easier to remember as a stack than as a
list, because each one captures a layer the one above it
takes for granted. @fig-five-pillars is that stack.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-five-pillars
%%| fig-alt: "Five layers stacked bottom to top, each depending on
%%|   the one below. From the bottom: the Dockerfile supplying
%%|   operating system, system libraries and the R build; renv.lock
%%|   pinning every R package version; .Rprofile activating the
%%|   project library; the source code in R/ and analysis/; and at
%%|   the top the data, raw and derived or a documented path to
%%|   it."
%%| fig-cap: "The Five Pillars as a layered stack. Each layer
%%|   assumes the one beneath it. Remove the Dockerfile and the R
%%|   packages have no operating system to install onto; remove the
%%|   lockfile and the source code has no packages; remove the data
%%|   and there is nothing to analyze."
flowchart TD
  D["<b>5. Data</b><br/><i>raw and derived, or a documented path to them</i>"]
  S["<b>4. Source code</b><br/><i>the analysis, in R/ and analysis/</i>"]
  P["<b>3. .Rprofile</b><br/><i>activates the project library</i>"]
  L["<b>2. renv.lock</b><br/><i>every R package version</i>"]
  F["<b>1. Dockerfile</b><br/><i>operating system, system libraries, R build</i>"]
  F --> L --> P --> S --> D
```

**Pillar 1: Dockerfile.** Captures the OS and
system libraries below R. Without it, an analysis
that depends on `libgdal` or a specific BLAS
implementation reproduces only on machines with
those libraries pre-installed. The
`zzcollab`-generated Dockerfile pins the rocker
base image by tag and, when Docker can resolve it,
by digest (for example
`rocker/r-ver:4.6.0@sha256:...`), and installs the
system libraries the project's R packages need.

**Pillar 2: `renv.lock`.** Records the R version
and every R package version, including transitive
dependencies; the R installation itself comes from
the Dockerfile. Without it, package updates between
the analysis run and the reproduction silently
change behavior.

**Pillar 3: `.Rprofile`.** A project-local R
startup file that activates `renv`'s project
library. Without it, opening the project in a
fresh R session loads the user's global library,
defeating `renv`'s isolation.

**Pillar 4: Source code.** The analysis itself,
in `R/` (helpers) and `analysis/` (scripts and
narrative). Version-controlled in git from day
one.

**Pillar 5: Data.** Raw and processed data, or a
documented procedure for obtaining them.
Sensitive data often cannot live in the compendium
directly; in that case, the compendium contains a
README documenting the access path, in the form
@sec-federal will set out.

The five pillars are a checklist. Every project
should satisfy each; `make check-renv` and a quick
manual audit verify that they do.

## Profiles and bundles

The command `zzc <profile>`, run inside an empty project
directory, scaffolds a project using one of four
profiles. Each profile is defined in
`templates/bundles.yaml`, and its main job is to choose
the rocker base image:

| Profile      | Base image         | Approximate size | Use                            |
| ------------ | ------------------ | ---------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `minimal`    | `rocker/r-ver`     | 650 MB           | command-line work, CI          |
| `tidyverse`  | `rocker/tidyverse` | 1.2 GB           | tidyverse data analysis        |
| `rstudio`    | `rocker/rstudio`   | 980 MB           | RStudio Server development     |
| `publishing` | `rocker/verse`     | 4.2 GB           | manuscripts that need LaTeX    |

The `tidyverse` profile was formerly called `analysis`,
and `zzc analysis` still works as a deprecated alias.
There are no modeling or Shiny profiles; for those needs
the framework's own advice is to start from one of the
four and add packages inside the container.

Choosing among them:

- **`minimal`.** When you want to add packages
  one at a time. Useful for teaching examples or
  for projects with tight package budgets.
- **`tidyverse`.** Default for descriptive,
  exploratory, and tidyverse-heavy work.
- **`rstudio`.** When collaborators will work in a
  browser rather than a terminal.
- **`publishing`.** When the deliverable is a
  rendered PDF manuscript. The LaTeX layer is large
  but avoids installing TeX at render time.

Modeling packages need no special profile. Install
`lme4` or `survival` inside the container, record them
with `make snapshot`, and rebuild with
`make docker-build`. When zzcollab generates the
Dockerfile it reads the packages your code, `DESCRIPTION`,
and `renv.lock` mention and adds the system libraries
they need, so a profile mismatch costs a rebuild rather
than a hand-edited `apt-get` line.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: profile choice

**Question.** You are scaffolding a project that
will fit a Cox proportional hazards model with
`survival::coxph()` and a mixed-effects model with
`lme4::glmer()`, then render the result as a PDF
manuscript. Which profile?

**Answer.**

`publishing`, because the PDF manuscript is the one
requirement a profile actually supplies: it is the
only profile whose base image includes LaTeX. The
modeling packages are not a profile question at all.
Install `lme4` and `survival` inside the container,
run `make snapshot` so that `renv.lock` and
`DESCRIPTION` record them, and rebuild. Neither
package needs an extra system library; `survival` is a
recommended package that ships with R.

:::

## The first-project walkthrough

The minimum viable `zzcollab` session:

```bash
mkdir penguins-analysis
cd penguins-analysis
zzc tidyverse             # scaffold (Five Pillars appear)
make r                    # enter R session inside Docker
                          # ... do analysis ...
make check-renv           # validate dependencies
make docker-render-qmd    # render the Quarto report
```

What happens at each step:

**`zzc tidyverse`** runs the framework's
scaffolding. After it completes, the directory
contains a `DESCRIPTION`, `R/`, `analysis/`, and
`tests/` directories, a Quarto report at
`analysis/report/index.qmd`, a minimal `renv.lock`, a
`Dockerfile` on the `rocker/tidyverse` base, and a
`Makefile`. It then offers to build the image. Git is
a separate step (`zzc git`, or `git init` yourself).

**`make r`** drops you into an interactive R session
inside the container, with the project directory
mounted, so files edited inside the container persist
on the host. It does not build the image; if no image
exists it says so and falls back to R on the host.
Build first with `make docker-build` if you declined at
scaffolding time.

**`make check-renv`** runs
`zzrenvcheck::check_packages(auto_fix = TRUE,
strict = TRUE)` on the host. It checks that the
packages your code uses, the packages `DESCRIPTION`
declares, and the packages `renv.lock` records all
agree, and with `auto_fix` it *edits* `DESCRIPTION` and
`renv.lock` to add what is missing. It is not a
read-only audit; use `make check-renv-no-fix` for a
report that changes nothing. It does not build the
Dockerfile or inspect `.Rprofile` or the data.

**`make docker-render-qmd`** runs
`quarto render analysis/report/index.qmd` inside the
container. (`make docker-render` renders an R Markdown
report instead, `analysis/report/report.Rmd` by
default.)

## The project `Makefile`

Every `zzcollab` project gets a `Makefile` with
many targets; `make help` lists them. The ones used
most:

| Target                   | Action                                              |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `make help`              | List all targets                                    |
| `make r`                 | Drop into R inside the project's container          |
| `make rstudio`           | Launch RStudio Server (port 8787)                   |
| `make docker-render-qmd` | Render `analysis/report/index.qmd` in the container |
| `make check-renv`        | Validate dependencies and add missing ones          |
| `make check-renv-no-fix` | Validate dependencies without modifying files       |
| `make snapshot`          | Snapshot `renv.lock` in the container, then validate |
| `make docker-build`      | Rebuild the image (use after adding packages)       |
| `make clean`             | Remove package build artifacts                      |

The non-obvious ones:

**`make rstudio`** for browser-based interactive
work. After `make rstudio`, open
`http://localhost:8787` in a browser and log in as
`rstudio` with the password `rstudio`, which the
target prints. The target publishes port 8787 on all
of your machine's network interfaces, so with that
fixed password, use it only on a trusted network (see
@sec-docker for binding to `127.0.0.1` instead).

**`make docker-build`** rebuilds the image after
you add packages or system dependencies. `make r`
silently uses the old image until you do.

**`make clean`** removes package build artifacts
(`*.tar.gz` and `*.Rcheck`); it does not touch rendered
reports or Quarto's `_freeze/` directory.

## How profiles are defined

`templates/bundles.yaml` has three sections.
`library_bundles` name sets of system packages,
`package_bundles` name sets of R packages, and
`profiles` combine a base image with one bundle of
each. An abbreviated entry:

```yaml
# templates/bundles.yaml (excerpt)

package_bundles:
  tidyverse:
    description: "Tidyverse ecosystem for data analysis"
    packages: [renv, devtools, tidyverse, here]
    requires_libs: ["minimal"]

profiles:
  tidyverse:
    description: "Data analysis with tidyverse"
    base_image: "rocker/tidyverse"
    libs: minimal
    pkgs: tidyverse
    size: "~1.2GB"
```

There is no `inherits` key, and in the current version
the quickstart command accepts only the four built-in
profile names. A group that wants different defaults
can add a profile entry in a fork and select it with
`zzc docker --profile <name>`, but the Dockerfile
generator reads only the entry's `base_image`; the
system libraries come from the packages the project
uses, as described above, and R packages are added
inside the container and recorded with
`make snapshot`. Group conventions therefore live
mostly in a template project or a shared `renv.lock`,
not in a new profile. Check the repository's current
`bundles.yaml` before relying on any of this, since the
schema has changed between versions.

## When `zzcollab` is not the right tool

`zzcollab` is overkill for:

- **Interactive exploration.** Just open RStudio.
- **One-off scripts.** Just write a script.
- **Teaching examples whose point is the code,
  not the infrastructure.** Less infrastructure
  is clearer.
- **Quick reproductions of someone else's
  analysis.** Their existing structure should
  control.

It is the right tool for: collaborative analyses
that will be passed between team members,
analyses that must survive for months or years
after the lead analyst has moved on, and any
analysis subject to the federal requirements taken
up in @sec-federal.

The 'right level of infrastructure' is itself a
judgment. Excessive infrastructure on a small
project is busywork; insufficient infrastructure
on a large one is technical debt. `zzcollab`
makes the high-infrastructure path cheap, which
shifts the right answer toward more
infrastructure on the margin.

## Collaborating with an LLM on `zzcollab`

LLMs handle the framework well; the trap is
generic 'set up a research project' suggestions
that ignore the framework's existence.

**Prompt 1: auditing an analysis against the Five
Pillars.** Paste a directory listing and ask: 'map
this project onto the Five Pillars (Dockerfile,
renv.lock, .Rprofile, source code, data). What is
missing from each, and what would I need to add?'
The audit is tool-neutral: the answer is the same
whether you then add the files by hand, with
`rrtools`, or with `zzcollab`.

*What to watch for.* The LLM should identify
each pillar concretely (Dockerfile present?
renv.lock? `.Rprofile`? Source code? Data?). If
it generates abstract guidance instead, push for
the file-by-file inventory.

*Verification.* Check each claimed pillar yourself:
open the file, and for the Dockerfile and lockfile,
build and restore them. Optionally run `zzc tidyverse`
in a scratch directory and compare its structure to
your project.

**Prompt 2: comparing frameworks.** Describe a
project type and ask the LLM to compare
`zzcollab`, `rrtools`, and `workflowr`.

*What to watch for.* Each framework has a niche.
`zzcollab` is opinionated and fast; `rrtools` is
flexible; `workflowr` emphasizes the analysis
website. The LLM should not declare a winner; it
should match each to a use case.

*Verification.* Cross-reference each framework's
README; if the LLM's claims about features are
correct, the comparison is reliable.

**Prompt 3: designing a package set.** Describe a
niche (e.g., neuroimaging, RNA-seq,
electrophysiology). Ask: 'list the R packages and
system libraries a project in this niche typically
needs.'

*What to watch for.* The system libraries
(neuroimaging needs FSL or AFNI tooling;
RNA-seq often needs `Bioconductor` packages
plus their `apt-get` dependencies). The LLM
should produce plausible candidates; verify
against domain documentation.

*Verification.* In a scratch project, install the
packages inside the container, run `make snapshot`,
and rebuild with `make docker-build`. The build
either succeeds or surfaces missing dependencies
(which you then add).

## Principle in use

Three habits keep the framework proportionate to the
project:

1. **Pick the right profile up front.** Profile
   mismatches are recoverable but slow. Match
   profile to project type from day one.
2. **Audit before deposition.** `make
   check-renv` plus a manual Pillar inventory
   before submitting or archiving.
3. **Extend deliberately, not promiscuously.** A
   custom bundle for genuine group conventions;
   not for every one-off project.

## Exercises

**On your own machine, data, or collaborations.** These exercises create
projects on disk, so no answer key is possible.

1. Scaffold a `zzcollab` analysis project for
   the Palmer Penguins dataset. Run `make r`,
   load the data, produce a single scatter
   plot, and save it to `analysis/`.
2. Take an existing analysis of yours and
   migrate it into a `zzcollab` compendium.
   Confirm every Pillar is present and run
   `make check-renv` to validate.
3. Assemble the package set for your research
   niche (e.g., 'survival analysis with heavy
   tidymodels use') in a scratch `zzcollab`
   project, record it with `make snapshot`, and
   reuse that lockfile to start a real project.
4. Compare the time to set up a project from
   scratch with `rrtools` vs. with
   `zzc tidyverse`. Time both. Document the
   difference.
5. Use `make rstudio` to launch RStudio Server
   in a `zzcollab` container; access it from a
   browser; render an analysis from inside the
   browser session. Confirm the result matches
   `make docker-render-qmd` from the terminal.

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-10}

1. The Five Pillars are: (1) a **Dockerfile**
   (captures OS and system libs), (2) an
   **renv.lock** (captures R package versions),
   (3) an **.Rprofile** (activates renv and sets
   project-local R options), (4) **source code**
   (the actual analysis), and (5) **data** (raw
   and processed, or DOI pointers when data
   cannot be shared). Each pillar captures a
   layer that the others do not: Docker covers
   the OS below R, `renv` covers R itself,
   `.Rprofile` covers R's runtime configuration,
   source code is the work product, and data is
   the input. Remove any one and the analysis
   cannot be reproduced.
2. `zzcollab` *wraps* `renv` and Docker and
   *follows* `rrtools`. It does not call `rrtools`;
   it writes its own directory layout, modeled on
   the Marwick, Boettiger, and Mullen compendium
   that `rrtools` implements. It uses `renv` for
   R package management and Docker for the
   environment, and adds profile-based base images
   (four profiles), a build system (`Makefile`),
   and validation commands (`make check-renv`). It
   does not replace `renv` or Docker; it removes
   the manual wiring between them.
3. A profile chiefly determines the rocker base
   image: `rocker/r-ver` for `minimal`,
   `rocker/tidyverse` for `tidyverse` (formerly
   `analysis`), `rocker/rstudio` for `rstudio`,
   and `rocker/verse` for `publishing`. Choose
   `publishing` when the deliverable is a PDF
   manuscript, because only its base includes
   LaTeX; otherwise `tidyverse` gives a much
   smaller image. Modeling packages are added
   inside the container under any profile.
